poems:
5:00. The chair is still warm.
He is already in the parking deck.

One minute in and the on-ramp is not a ramp.
It is a parking lot with ambitions.
A daycare door propped with a cinder block.

Onions, garlic, a pound of ground chuck.
The list does not mention bread.
It never mentions bread.
The mower on the trailer, still ticking.
5:05. Someone's second gin, poured at what they have decided is a reasonable hour.

Apron over the head. Strings crossed in back, tied in front.
The first ticket prints before the knot is finished.
I'm five minutes out, he says, from the wrong side of the bridge.
Crossing guard's vest folded on the passenger seat.

A woman crosses the parking lot at a run
in dress shoes,
carrying nothing,
which is the fastest way to run.

Rush hour, noun: a period of sixty to one hundred forty minutes,
named by a person who was not in it.
Somebody's dog has been alone since seven and has an opinion about it.
5:12. The oven preheats to a temperature nobody will verify.

Backpack in the hall. Shoes in the hall.
Child upstairs, reporting no knowledge of either.
Brake lights, four lanes, all the way to the interchange.
Quarter past. The bartender cuts limes for the people who are still merging.
A pallet jack against a wall, handle up.
5:17 and the meeting that was going to end at five is discovering new business.

The daycare charges a dollar a minute after six.
Everybody on this road knows the number.

Two eggs, one onion, whatever is in the door of the fridge.
This is a plan, technically.

Somewhere it has already gone gray. Somewhere it has not.
Either way the pans come out.
5:21. The cat has decided this is dinner and is being clear about it.
Line cook, tasting spoon, garbage can. Repeat.
The train doors close on a coat sleeve, then think better of it.
A stroller folded against the wall of a bus shelter.

5:25. Whatever you were going to finish today,
you are now going to finish tomorrow.
The bus kneels. Three people get off. It stands back up.

5:27. Somebody's phone says forty-one minutes,
which is a lie it has told before.

You have reached the front desk. Our office closed at five.
Please call back during regular business hours.
A man in a suit jacket buys a lottery ticket and a banana.

Half past. The pot goes on. The kid is called once,
which everyone understands to be the first of three.
The playground empties in the order parents arrive.
5:32. The gym door opens, closes, opens.

House red, 9.00
House red, 9.00
Subtotal 18.00
Tip line blank, still thinking
Traffic voices on the radio, naming roads you are already on.
A hose coiled by a spigot, dripping.

5:36. The onions have gone translucent, which is the only part
of the recipe anyone can watch happen.

Somebody is doing algebra at a kitchen counter
while somebody else moves the plates around it.

The last meeting of the day has a hard stop.
So does the person waiting in the pickup line.
Two forklifts, nose to nose, negotiating.
5:40. The bar fills the way a bathtub fills, from one end.

Pull to the curb. Do not exit the vehicle.
A teacher will bring your child to you.
Do not exit the vehicle.

A hospital elevator holds for a food cart.
Everybody waits. The cart is not in a hurry.

5:43. Nobody has decided about dinner.
Everybody has opinions about what it should not be.

The dishwasher from last night is still clean and full,
which everybody has agreed not to mention.

Quarter to six. The dog is at the door
because a car sounded like the right car.
Folding chair on a lawn, facing the road.

5:47. The commuter who left early is now in the same place
as the commuter who left late.

Somebody's kettle.
Somebody's shower.
Somebody's news at a volume
chosen for a different room.

The pickup line has moved three cars in nine minutes.
This counts as progress.
Ten to. The apron pockets get their pens.
A bike leaned on a rail outside a restaurant, unlocked.
5:52. The stock is doing what stock does, which is not much, visibly.

Homework.
Laundry.
The thing about the permission slip.
One of these is getting done.
The last typing in the office, audible now.
5:55. Enough time to start nothing.

A child asleep in a car seat in a driveway,
and nobody wants to be the one to move her.
Grease pencil on the specials board. Two items crossed out already.

The garage door goes up. Whatever happened today
is now a story with an audience.

One minute to six. The pan is hot
and the fish is not out of its paper yet.
